0.title: Pictures of God
0.essay:
No one has ever seen God. Yet the Bible is full of pictures of him: a rock, a shepherd, a father, a light, a fire, a husband. God, who is beyond all our thoughts, has chosen to show us who he is in words a child can understand.

Why God speaks in pictures

“God is spirit” (John 4:24). He has no body, no shape and no size. He “dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see” (1 Timothy 6:16). If God had spoken to us only in exact theological terms, we would have learned true things about him, but we would have struggled to feel them, remember them or lean on them when life is hard. So God stoops. He takes things we know, a rock under our feet, bread on the table, a father’s arms, and says, “I am like this.” John Calvin compared this to a nurse speaking simply to a small child: God lowers his speech to our level, not because he is small, but because we are.

How to read the pictures rightly

Each picture is true. God really is a rock, a refuge and a light, because he has said so. But each picture is also partial. A rock is strong but cannot love. A father loves but grows old. A fire purifies but can seem only fearsome. No single picture is the whole of God, and if we take one and forget the rest we will soon have a lopsided God. So the pictures correct and complete one another. The King is also a Father. The consuming fire is also the husband who rejoices over his bride. We must hold them together, and let the plain teaching of Scripture govern how far each picture goes.

Pictures given, not images made

There is a great difference between pictures God gives in words and images we make with our hands. The second commandment forbids us to make “a carved image, or any likeness” (Exodus 20:4) to worship. At Sinai Israel “saw no form” (Deuteronomy 4:15), only heard a voice. God chooses how he is to be pictured, and he has chosen words. The study The Ten Commandments explains this commandment more fully. Word-pictures leave God free and mysterious; a carved or painted image shrinks him to our size.

All of them meet in Christ

Every picture finds its fullest meaning in Jesus Christ, who is “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). He is the Rock, the Light, the Bread, the Bridegroom, the King and the Judge. That is where this study will end.

The chapters

Rock, Refuge and Wings; Father, Potter and Host; Light, Water and Bread; King, Judge and Warrior; Husband, Redeemer and Friend; and The Image of the Invisible God.

For reflection

Which picture of God first comes to mind when you think of him? Is there a picture in Scripture you tend to forget or avoid, and why might that be?

1.title: Rock, Refuge and Wings
1.essay:
When David looked for words to describe what God had been to him in years of danger, he reached for the landscape of the wilderness where he had hidden: rocks, cliffs, strongholds, shields. Then he went further and spoke of wings.

The Rock

In the song of Moses God is simply called “The Rock”: “The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he” (Deuteronomy 32:4). In a land of shifting sand and sudden floods, a rock does not move. So the picture speaks first of God’s faithfulness. He does not change his mind, wear out or let go.

David piles the pictures up in one breath: “The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold” (Psalm 18:2). He had hidden in the caves of En-gedi and on the heights of the wilderness while Saul hunted him. He knew that rocks could save his life. But he also knew that the cliffs were only a sign of the real shelter. Behind every rock was the LORD.

Isaiah tells us to “Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock” (Isaiah 26:4). And the New Testament shows us who the Rock was all along. When Israel drank water from the rock in the wilderness, Paul says, “they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The rock that was struck so the people could drink points to the Saviour who was struck so that we might live.

Fortress, refuge and strong tower

A fortress is a rock with walls: a place built to hold out against an enemy. A refuge is wherever you run when danger comes. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way” (Psalm 46:1–2). The psalm does not promise that the earth will not give way. It promises that God will still be there when it does.

Proverbs adds a picture from the walled city: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10). Notice the verb. The righteous man runs. A tower protects only those who go into it. God’s name, all that he has revealed himself to be, is a place to flee to in prayer, not merely a fact to admire from outside.

And God is a shield. He said to Abram, “Fear not, Abram, I am your shield” (Genesis 15:1). David, surrounded by enemies, prayed, “But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head” (Psalm 3:3). A shield is held close and moves wherever the blow comes from.

The shadow of his wings

Then the pictures turn from stone to feathers. “Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 17:8). “He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler” (Psalm 91:4). A rock is strong but cold. Wings are strong and warm. The God who is a fortress is also as near and tender as a bird sheltering her young.

Psalm 91 begins: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). The promise belongs to the one who dwells there, who makes God his home, not only his emergency exit.

The eagle

One more picture of strength and care comes from the song of Moses. God led Israel through the wilderness “Like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that flutters over its young, spreading out its wings, catching them, bearing them on its pinions” (Deuteronomy 32:11). At Sinai God had already said, “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (Exodus 19:4). The nest is stirred up: comfort is disturbed, and the young must learn to fly. But the parent bird is underneath. God sometimes unsettles his people, but never to drop them. “Underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deuteronomy 33:27).

What these pictures do not promise

These pictures do not mean that believers will never be hurt. David wrote Psalm 18 after years of running for his life. Christians fall ill, lose jobs and suffer injustice. What the pictures promise is that nothing can reach us except through God’s hands, that he will hold us through it, and that nothing can take away what he has given us in Christ. In the end the Rock holds, the tower stands and the wings cover.

An example

A woman in her sixties received a hard diagnosis on the same week her husband lost his job. She found she could not pray long prayers. So she prayed one line from Psalm 61 over and over: “Lead me to the rock that is higher than I” (Psalm 61:2). It did not change the scan results. But it gave her somewhere to stand, and it reminded her that the God who held her was larger than the news that frightened her.

For reflection

What do you tend to run to first when trouble comes? Why do you think Scripture puts the hard picture of a rock beside the soft picture of wings? What is the difference between visiting the shelter of the Most High and dwelling there? How does knowing that “the Rock was Christ” deepen these pictures for you?

2.title: Father, Potter and Host
2.essay:
Strength is not enough. A fortress can keep you alive without caring whether you are happy. So Scripture gives us pictures of God that speak of tenderness, provision and patient shaping: a shepherd, a father, a mother’s comfort, a potter, a gardener and a host.

The shepherd

The best loved of all these pictures is the shepherd: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psalm 23:1). We will not go over it again here, because the study The Lord Is My Shepherd follows it from the real sheep of the hillside to the Good Shepherd who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). It is enough to say that the shepherd picture holds together strength and care: the rod for the wolf, the gentle hand for the lamb.

The Father

In the Old Testament God is sometimes called the Father of Israel. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:13–14).

But when Jesus came, the word “Father” moved to the centre. He taught his disciples to pray, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9). This is more than a picture. The eternal Son has always been the Son of the Father, and through faith in him we are adopted into that family. “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Abba is the warm, everyday Aramaic word a child used of his father. The Creator of the galaxies is the Father of every believer, and he knows how to give good gifts: “how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11).

Some people find this picture hard because their own father was absent, cold or cruel. God is not like that father. He is the Father every earthly father was meant to reflect and none has fully been. The picture is not drawn from our fathers upward. It runs the other way: all true fatherhood is a faint copy of his.

The comfort of a mother

Scripture also compares God’s love to a mother’s. “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). “As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you” (Isaiah 66:13). And Jesus, weeping over Jerusalem, said, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37).

These are precious, and we should not be embarrassed by them. But notice how they are worded: they are similes. God comforts “as” a mother, gathers “as” a hen. He is never named Mother, and no one in Scripture prays to him as Mother. God is spirit and is neither male nor female; the name Father does not mean he has a body or is a man. But the names are his to give. He has revealed himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit (see the study The Trinity), and we call him what he calls himself. The mother similes show us how tender that Father is. They do not give us a different name to use.

The potter

“But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand” (Isaiah 64:8). Isaiah joins the potter to the father. Jeremiah was sent to watch a potter at his wheel. When a pot was spoiled, the potter “reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do” (Jeremiah 18:4). God said, “like the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand” (Jeremiah 18:6).

The picture is humbling. Clay does not argue with the potter (Romans 9:20–21). God is sovereign over us, and he has the right to shape our lives as he sees best. But it is also hopeful. A spoiled pot is not thrown away; it is reworked. Our failures do not put us beyond his skilful hands.

The vinedresser

Jesus said, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–2). A vinedresser cuts. To the branch it must feel like loss. But a good gardener never prunes carelessly, and never to kill. He prunes because he expects fruit. The Father’s discipline of his children is like this: “he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10).

The host

Finally, God spreads a table. “You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows” (Psalm 23:5). In the ancient world a host who welcomed a guest to his table was bound to protect him. God does not merely keep us alive. He welcomes us, honours us and fills our cup to overflowing, and one day he will seat us at the marriage supper of the Lamb.

An example

A young man who had grown up with a violent father avoided the Lord’s Prayer for years; the word “Father” made him tense. A pastor read Psalm 103 with him and Luke 15, where the father “ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). Slowly he began to see that God was not a bigger version of the man he had feared, but the Father he had always needed. He still found it hard some days, but he kept praying the words until they began to feel like home.

For reflection

How has your own experience of a father shaped the way you think about God? Why is it important that the mother pictures are similes and not names? Where might the Father be pruning or reshaping you just now? What does it mean to you that God is a host who welcomes you to his table?

3.title: Light, Water and Bread
3.essay:
Some pictures of God are about protection and care. Others are about life itself. Without light, water and food we die. Scripture takes these most basic needs and says: God is all of these to the soul.

God is light

“The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 27:1). Light lets us see. In the dark we stumble, imagine dangers that are not there and miss the ones that are. When God is our light, we see things as they truly are, and fear loses its grip.

But light also means purity. “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). There is no shadow in God, no hidden motive, no flicker of evil. That is wonderful and also searching. Light exposes. John goes on to say that if we claim fellowship with God while walking in darkness, we lie (1 John 1:6). The study The Holiness of God explores this side of the picture. The light that guides us is the same light that shows up our sin, and both are mercies.

Then Jesus stood in the temple courts and said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). John had already told us: “In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (John 1:4–5). And Paul says that God “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Sun and shield

One psalm puts two pictures side by side: “For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly” (Psalm 84:11). The sun gives warmth, light and growth; the shield gives protection. God is both the source of every good thing and the defence against every harm.

The fountain of living waters

In the dry hills of Israel, water was life. A spring of fresh, flowing water, what the Bible calls “living water”, was worth more than gold. Cisterns, pits cut into rock to hold rainwater, were a poor second: the water went stale, and if the plaster cracked it drained away.

So God’s complaint through Jeremiah is sharp: “my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13). This is the picture of every idol. We leave the spring and spend our strength digging holes that cannot hold what we pour into them: money, approval, pleasure, success. The tragedy is not only that sin is wrong, but that it is foolish. We trade a fountain for a leaking pit.

“For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light” (Psalm 36:9). Jesus met a woman at a well who had tried many cisterns, and offered her something else: “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14).

The bread of life

After feeding five thousand people, Jesus told the crowds who came back for more: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). They wanted bread that would fill them until tomorrow. He offered himself, bread that would fill them for ever. The manna in the wilderness came down from heaven each morning; Jesus is the true bread from heaven, and he gives his flesh “for the life of the world” (John 6:51). We feed on him by faith, and the Lord’s Supper is a visible sign of that feeding.

The dew

One of the gentlest pictures in the Bible comes at the end of Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful again and again. God had said their love was “like the dew that goes early away” (Hosea 6:4), gone by mid-morning. Yet at the end he promises, “I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon” (Hosea 14:5).

In a land with a long dry summer, the night dew kept plants alive. It falls quietly, unseen, every night, and in the morning everything is fresh. Our love for God is like the dew that vanishes. His love for us is like the dew that returns. He does not usually renew his people with thunder, but with quiet, daily grace.

An example

A man in his forties had reached every goal he had set: a senior job, a good house, a respected name. He was surprised to find himself empty. A friend read him Jeremiah 2:13, and he recognised his life in it: years of digging cisterns. He did not quit his job. But he began to come to Christ each morning with his Bible before he opened his email, and found that the thirst he had tried to fill with achievement was being met at last.

For reflection

Where does God’s light comfort you, and where does it unsettle you? What “broken cisterns” are you most tempted to dig? What does it mean, in practice, to come to Christ as bread and water each day? How does the picture of the dew encourage someone whose love for God feels weak?

4.title: King, Judge and Warrior
4.essay:
Some pictures of God are comfortable. Others make us catch our breath. God is a King on a throne, a Judge who will do right, a Warrior who goes out to battle and a fire that consumes. These are pictures many people would prefer to leave out. Scripture does not.

The King

“For the LORD, the Most High, is to be feared, a great king over all the earth” (Psalm 47:2). “God reigns over the nations; God sits on his holy throne” (Psalm 47:8). Paul sings of “the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God” (1 Timothy 1:17). He rules everything, everywhere, always.

When Isaiah saw this King in the temple, he cried out, “Woe is me! For I am lost … for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!” (Isaiah 6:5). The picture of the King calls for awe and obedience. It also brings deep comfort. If God is King, then no tyrant, disease or chance has the last word. The study The Attributes of God explores his sovereignty further.

The Judge

When Abraham pleaded for Sodom he asked, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). He knew the answer. God “is a righteous judge” (Psalm 7:11). He sees every act and every motive. He cannot be bribed, fooled or worn down. Every wrong ever done will one day be brought before him.

The Warrior

After the Red Sea, Moses and Israel sang, “The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name” (Exodus 15:3). Israel had not fought. God had fought for them. And at the end of the Bible the Warrior rides out: “I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war” (Revelation 19:11). He is Christ himself.

The consuming fire

“For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God” (Deuteronomy 4:24). The letter to the Hebrews repeats it to Christians: “let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29). Fire gives light and warmth; it also burns up whatever cannot stand it. God’s holiness is like that. It purifies what belongs to him and consumes what opposes him. The study The Fear of the Lord shows how this fire leads not to terror but to reverent, joyful worship.

Good news for the oppressed

Why are these pictures in the Bible? First, because they are good news for the weak. “The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed” (Psalm 9:9). If there were no Judge, the abuser, the trafficker and the tyrant would get away with it for ever. The cheated widow and the harmed child need to know that God is a righteous Judge who fights for the helpless. A God who never judged would not be kind; he would be indifferent to evil. These pictures tell the oppressed that their cries are heard and that justice is coming.

Terrible for the unrepentant

But the same pictures are terrible for those who will not turn. “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31). Scripture urges, “Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way” (Psalm 2:12). The King will not always wait. The fire that warms the humble will burn the proud. We do not soften this; God’s warnings are a mercy, given so that we may flee to him while there is time.

The Judge judged in our place

And here the gospel shines brightest. If God is a just Judge, how can any of us stand? We have all broken his law. The answer is the cross. The Judge himself came down, in the person of his Son, and stood in the dock in our place. “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5). “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

So God is not just in spite of saving us; he is just in saving us, because the penalty has been paid in full. He is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The fire fell on Christ. The Warrior fought our true enemies, sin, death and the devil, and at the cross he “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). For everyone who trusts in Christ, the King is our Father, the Judge has declared us righteous, the Warrior fights for us and the fire is a wall of protection around us (Zechariah 2:5).

An example

A woman who had been badly treated by a former employer carried bitterness for years. She felt that if she let it go, no one would ever hold him to account. Reading Genesis 18:25 helped her. She saw that she did not need to be the judge, because the Judge of all the earth would do right. She reported what needed reporting, and then handed the rest to God. She also found herself praying, to her surprise, that the man might find mercy at the cross before he met the Judge.

For reflection

Why do you think many people today avoid the pictures of God as Judge and Warrior? How is the justice of God good news for those who suffer wrong? What does it mean for you that the Judge was judged in your place? How should Hebrews 12:28–29 shape the way you come to worship?

5.title: Husband, Redeemer and Friend
5.essay:
The most intimate pictures of God in the Bible are pictures of relationship. God binds himself to his people by covenant, a solemn promise that makes them his own. To show what that means, he speaks of a husband and bride, a kinsman who redeems and a friend who speaks face to face.

Your Maker is your husband

To a people who felt abandoned in exile, God said, “For your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name; and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer” (Isaiah 54:5). Later he promised, “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). God does not merely tolerate his people. He delights in them as a bridegroom delights in his bride on their wedding day.

The faithful husband and the unfaithful wife

The picture also exposes sin. Throughout the prophets, Israel’s idolatry is called adultery. Jeremiah 3 describes Israel as a wife who has left her husband for many lovers. Yet even there God pleads, “Return, O faithless children, declares the LORD; for I am your master; I will take you” (Jeremiah 3:14).

Hosea was told to live out the picture in his own home. He married Gomer, who was unfaithful to him. Then God said, “Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods” (Hosea 3:1). Hosea bought her back. This is how God loves: not because his bride is lovely, but to make her lovely. “I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her” (Hosea 2:14). “I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy” (Hosea 2:19).

Christ and his bride

In the New Testament the Bridegroom is Christ. “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Paul goes on to say that marriage is a picture of something greater: “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). God did not invent the gospel to fit marriage. He made marriage to point to the gospel. (The study Christian Marriage works this out for husbands and wives.)

And history ends with a wedding. “Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).

A jealous God

Because God is a husband, he is jealous. “You shall worship no other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exodus 34:14). Many people stumble at this word, because human jealousy is often petty, insecure and controlling. But there is a right jealousy too. A husband who did not care if his wife gave herself to other men would not be loving; he would be indifferent. God’s jealousy is not envy of what belongs to someone else. It is his burning zeal for what rightly belongs to him, the whole-hearted love of his people, because he knows that every rival will destroy them. Paul felt “a divine jealousy” for the Corinthian church, because he had betrothed them “to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). God’s jealousy is love that will not share us with what would ruin us.

The Redeemer

Isaiah joins husband and redeemer together. “Fear not, you worm Jacob … your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel” (Isaiah 41:14). In Israel a redeemer, often called a kinsman-redeemer, was a close relative who stepped in when a family member was in trouble: buying back land that had been sold, freeing a relative sold into slavery, or keeping a dead man’s name alive by marrying his widow.

The book of Ruth shows this beautifully. Ruth, a poor foreign widow, came to Boaz and said, “Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer” (Ruth 3:9). Boaz paid the price, married her and brought her into the family. The women said to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer” (Ruth 4:14). Ruth became the great-grandmother of David, and so an ancestor of Jesus.

Christ is our kinsman-redeemer. To redeem us he had to become our kinsman, sharing our flesh and blood. Then he paid the price, not with silver, but with his own blood. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

The Friend

Finally, God is a friend. “Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11). Abraham “was called a friend of God” (James 2:23). And Jesus said to his disciples, “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). A friend shares his heart. Christ has told us his Father’s purposes. And he proved his friendship in the greatest way: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

This friendship never makes God our equal. He remains our King and Lord, and Jesus adds, “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). But it does mean that the Lord of glory wants our company.

An example

A man who had been unfaithful to his wife came back to Christ deeply ashamed. He assumed God would at best put up with him from a distance. Reading Hosea changed that. He saw that God had pursued a people far more unfaithful than he, and bought them back. It did not make his sin small. But it gave him the courage to repent fully, to his wife and to God, and to believe that he could be loved again.

For reflection

How does the picture of God as a husband change the way you think about sin? What is the difference between God’s jealousy and sinful human jealousy? Why did Christ need to become our kinsman in order to redeem us? What does it mean to you that Jesus calls you his friend?

6.title: The Image of the Invisible God
6.essay:
All the pictures we have looked at are words. In Jesus Christ, God gave us more than words. He gave us a person: one who could be seen, heard and touched. Every picture in Scripture finds its fullest meaning in him.

The image of the invisible God

“No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). Paul says of Christ, “He is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). Hebrews says, “He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3). As light streams from the sun, the Son shines out the glory of the Father. As a seal leaves its exact shape in wax, so the Son bears the very nature of God.

When Philip asked to see the Father, Jesus replied, “Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus: his compassion for the leper, his patience with the slow disciples, his anger at hypocrisy, his tears at a grave, his forgiveness of the thief. God is not different from Jesus, hidden behind him. In Jesus we see the Father’s heart.

This is why we do not need, and should not make, images of God or of Christ for worship. God has already given his own image, the living Son, and he has given us a faithful portrait of him in the Gospels. This commentary follows the Reformed view that images of Christ should not be used in worship or as aids to prayer. Many Christians believe that because Christ took a real body he may rightly be depicted; but any picture of him is invented, and the Christ we need is the one Scripture shows us.

The “I am” sayings

In John’s Gospel Jesus takes many of the Old Testament pictures of God and applies them to himself. “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). “I am the door” (John 10:9). “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). Each one echoes God’s own name, “I AM”, and each one takes a picture once used of the LORD and says: it is me.

So we can trace the threads. The Rock is Christ, struck so that we might drink. The Shepherd is Christ, who lays down his life. The Light is Christ, shining in our hearts. The Bridegroom is Christ, who gave himself for his bride. The Redeemer is Christ, our kinsman. The Judge is Christ, who was judged for us and will come again to judge the living and the dead. The Warrior is Christ on the white horse. And the Father, whom the Son reveals, is the Father of all who are in Christ. The pictures do not compete. They are like light passing through a prism: one light, many colours.

Praying the pictures

The pictures were not given only for study. They were given for use. The psalmists show us how: they took a picture and prayed it. “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer” (Psalm 19:14). When you pray, address God by the picture you need. “Father, I am your child; help me.” “Lord, you are my refuge; I am running to you now.” “Lord Jesus, you are the bread of life; feed me today.”

Matching the picture to the need

Different seasons need different pictures. When you are afraid, remember the Rock, the fortress and the wings. When you are lonely, the Father, the Friend and the Bridegroom who rejoices over you. When you are confused, the Light. When you feel empty, the fountain and the bread. When you are wronged, the Judge who will do right. When you are proud or careless, the King and the consuming fire. When you have failed, the Potter who reworks the clay, the Husband who buys back his bride, the dew that returns. When you are suffering under God’s hand, the Vinedresser who prunes for fruit.

The mistake is to keep only one or two favourite pictures. The comforting pictures without the holy ones make God soft; the holy ones without the comforting make him harsh. A Christian who knows the whole gallery knows God better.

Worship and hard times

The pictures also feed worship. Many of the church’s best hymns and the psalms themselves are built on them, and singing them together fixes them in our memories for the day we will need them. In hard times we often cannot remember arguments, but we can remember a picture. A rock. A wing. A light in the dark. A table spread.

And one day pictures will no longer be needed. In the new creation “they will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). “The city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23). Every picture we now treasure will be outshone by the reality, and the reality will have the face of Jesus.

An example

A student far from home went through a dark winter of anxiety. Her doctor helped her, and she took the medicine she was prescribed. She also wrote a different picture of God on a card each week and kept it by her bed: “The LORD is my light” one week, “a strong tower” the next, then “the bread of life”. She found that the pictures gave her mind somewhere to rest at night, and that each one led her back to Christ.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father? Which of the “I am” sayings speaks most to you at present, and why? Which picture of God do you most need this week? How could you begin praying the pictures of God in your own prayers?
